drills.q: Walk through Azure's compute options from most to least control and name the decision axis that actually matters.
drills.a: VMs (full OS control) -> VMSS (fleet-managed VMs) -> App Service (PaaS, shared-plan capacity) -> Container Apps (serverless containers, scale-to-zero) -> AKS (full Kubernetes API). The real decision axis is how much orchestration complexity the team is willing to own versus how much control the workload genuinely needs -- not raw power.

drills.q: Why is deploying five unrelated apps to one App Service Plan risky, and how do you fix it?
drills.a: An App Service Plan is shared VM instance capacity across every app on it; a spike on one app competes for the same pool as the others, unlike per-invocation isolated billing. Fix: split apps with independent/unpredictable traffic onto separate plans, or move bursty apps to Container Apps.

drills.q: Explain the real difference between VMSS Flexible and Uniform orchestration modes.
drills.a: Uniform requires identical instances managed as one logical VMSS-API unit. Flexible mixes up to 5 different VM sizes (including Spot) in one scale set and integrates with standard Load Balancer/App Gateway backend pools like individual VMs -- Flexible is the 2026-recommended default, closing the heterogeneous-fleet gap.

drills.q: A customer-facing Container Apps API needs sub-300ms p99. Design it and state the cost tradeoff.
drills.a: Set minReplicas >= 1 so the app never scales to zero and never pays a cold-start tax on the customer path; scale-out rules handle growth above the warm floor. Tradeoff: continuous idle-rate billing for at least one replica, forfeiting pure scale-to-zero economics.

drills.q: Explain AKS Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP) and how it changes platform-team operational burden versus classic AKS.
drills.a: Classic AKS requires pre-configured node pools (SKU, min/max) plus a cluster autoscaler that scales within them. NAP watches for pending/unschedulable pods and provisions right-sized nodes just-in-time without pre-defined pool shapes -- the same bet as Karpenter/EKS Auto Mode. AKS Automatic bundles NAP with managed system node pools and a 99.9%-within-5-minutes pod readiness SLA.

drills.q: A subscription that has freely created AKS clusters for years suddenly can't create a new one. Diagnose.
drills.a: Starting September 2025, AKS enforces region-level quota on both managed cluster count and specific node VM SKUs, separate from the older per-cluster limits (5,000 nodes/cluster, 100 node pools/cluster). A subscription well under the old limits can still be blocked by this newer quota gate -- check the specific quota dimension, then request an increase.

drills.q: Compare Container Apps to AWS Fargate on the property that most changes cost modeling for spiky workloads.
drills.a: Container Apps scales to zero replicas and near-zero cost when idle; Fargate has no scale-to-zero -- minimum running task count is 1 whenever a service is active, billing continuously through idle periods. For spiky, low-average-utilization services this is a large realized cost delta favoring Container Apps, at the price of cold-start risk on the first post-idle request.

drills.q: Give a legitimate reason to choose AKS over Container Apps for a workload Container Apps could technically run.
drills.a: The workload needs custom Kubernetes CRDs/operators (service mesh, database operators managing StatefulSets), DaemonSets for node-level agents, fine-grained scheduling/affinity control beyond KEDA, or the team already operates AKS for other services and consolidating avoids a second compute paradigm -- raw power alone isn't sufficient justification given the added operational surface.

drills.q: Design compute for a stable predictable web tier plus a background-job tier that spikes 20x nightly.
drills.a: Web tier: App Service Premium v3 with deployment slots for zero-downtime releases -- predictable load suits fixed-capacity billing. Background tier: Container Apps with minReplicas:0 and a queue-depth KEDA scale rule -- near-zero cost 23 hours/day, fast scale-out during the nightly spike. Deliberately mixing compute paradigms by workload shape is the senior signal.

drills.q: A VMSS Flexible-mode deployment using a custom managed image fails approaching 600 instances. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: Managed-image-based VMSS instances cap at 600 versus 1,000 for images distributed via Azure Compute Gallery or marketplace images -- a frequently-missed caveat on the headline 1,000-instance number. Fix: migrate the custom image into Azure Compute Gallery.

drills.q: Explain the App Service deployment slot swap mechanism and one concrete way it silently causes production errors.
drills.a: A slot is a fully separate live app sharing plan compute; swap flips routing after warming up the target slot via applicationInitialization probes, in principle giving zero-downtime deploys. If warm-up isn't configured or doesn't cover real startup work (cache priming, connection pools, JIT), traffic routes to a not-actually-ready instance the moment the swap completes, producing an error burst right after a supposedly clean swap.
